en: The Commentary on the Samantakūṭa Chapter.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One,
whose fame is constant and far-reaching, and who has destroyed the arrogance of Kandappa.
I pay homage to the Sugata, the benefactor of the three worlds,
the unique banner of the entire universe, the one of immeasurable mind and priceless worth, the embodiment of peace,
the essence of Mount Meru, the noble one, and the essence of all forms.
The sun atop the mountain of the Buddha’s former [resolve] has destroyed the frost of evil deeds,
dispelled the heat of the mire of delusion, caused the lotus-like minds of all other beings to blossom,
and put to flight the night-lotuses of those with wicked thoughts.
I pay homage to the risen, sublime Sun of Dhamma,
whose pure virtue is complete, who has shaken off the thicket of evil,
and who is worthy of honor by gods and men, and worthy of hospitality and offerings.
With reverence, I pay homage to the assembly, who have entered the straight path, who are a field of merit for people,
and who are mature. May this prostration destroy all calamities.
I shall describe the king of mountains, Sumanasikhara,
purified by the descent upon its lotus-feet of the Sugata;
let the virtuous beings listen, for this incomparable abode is where the gods dwell.
Hearing, speaking, mindfulness, and also homage—
by these one becomes truly happy and attains Nibbāna.
Therefore, those seeking this triple perfection among the virtuous, [should practice them].
For with a mind that is to be heard by the virtuous and free from reproach,
you were born in the Tusita realm as one renowned as "Santusita," the Lord who is the ornament of the world, having fulfilled the ten perfections.
O Noble One, this Kāla has been propitiated by you through the gods and others;
having crossed over yourself, you shall ferry this world across—many who possess little dust in their eyes.
It was for this very purpose, O Hero, that the ten perfections were fulfilled by you.
"The world clings to you, as a son clings to his father's arm.
Having heard those words of theirs, the Great Being of great intelligence,
whose five eyes were stainless, looked out upon the world.
The city of Kapilavatthu was as delightful as the pericarp of the lotus that is the foremost land of Jambudīpa;
it possessed lofty peaks like the horns of the gods who consume ambrosia,
resembling the radiance of molten gold.
There was a palace adorned with a lion’s cage of jewels that shone as if hundreds of suns were constantly in the thick sky;
there stood a golden banner, shimmering like lightning stirred by the wind.
That city, where the faces of the people with their blue eyes bring forth splendor like golden jars adorned with honey-creepers; that city,
[resounding] with the neighing of tall, colorful horses and elephants.
Where the ocean’s peace was agitated by waves lofty with the sound of *sagho*,
resembling the arms of the gods as they called out from their cities,
and where various tall banners of many colors were stirred by gentle breezes.
Wearing various garments, adorned with various ornaments,
endowed with various excellences, and masters of various sciences;
they were unrestrained in their fresh youth and captivating in their beauty.
May there always be families devoted to the true Dhamma and free from reproach;
may that city be inhabited by men and women of noble character who are skilled in play and speak with sweet voices.
In that [lineage], there was one endowed with faith and other virtues,
the banner of the Okkāka clan, known by the name Śuddhodana, renowned throughout the three worlds;
he was like a white lotus among all the kings upon the earth.
As if constantly playing with the reflection of the crest-jewel [of the Buddha],
the sun— the leader of the world— was eclipsed by his expansive radiance,
and even the moon’s graceful movement across the sky during the day was surpassed.
For him whose flow of giving toward various supplicants crossed over their sevenfold nature like the ocean tide overflowing its shores,
who was like a wise counselor with his intellect and like the Giver of Wealth with his riches—
She who clung to him upon the earth as bees cling to flowers because of his beauty—
she was consecrated with sovereignty over him, she who was renowned as Mahāmāyā,
like Candi to the Moon, or like Girirājā to Kapila.
Like Lakṣmī to Vāsudeva, or Sītā to King Rāma, this queen of noble mien,
Sundarī with her beautiful lips, was the chief consort;
and within the vessel of her womb, like a priceless jewel, [was he].
Bewildering the world of gods and men with thirty-two marks,
that Holy One— like a white elephant with tusks like lotus stalks—
circumambulated his mother and entered her womb.
In this way, with eleven verses, such was her intention:
having gone to the city then to see her own kinsmen,
she reported that matter to the king, and by him [she was] well-prepared.
Then, traveling along the road with their retinue on the way,
they saw the garden named Lumbinī, which delighted the minds of the deities, resembling the Nandana grove, and bringing joy to the heart.
Eager to play, they entered that forest and approached a magnificent sal tree to sport;
it was strewn with swaying sprouts and bent low under its fully blossomed flowers.
Taking hold of a branch of the *sāla* tree, its young shoots being deep red,
Māyā gave birth there to her son, the Eye of the World, while the gods— including those of great power— held it as a protection for her amidst the assembly of devas.
Then the Brahmas, the World-Protectors,
and humans in succession took hold of the Delighter of Beings with golden nets, antelope skins, and other ornaments.
Having been established upon the earth, the Wise One then surveyed the directions.
Facing north, having taken seven steps upon a lotus and standing there,
he gazed at the quarters with eyes like full-blown lotuses and uttered these words, "The foremost, the best," and so forth.
Worshipped and venerated by Brahmās, gods, humans,
and others, increasing in splendor like the moon in its bright fortnight,
he dwelt beneath the shade of the Brahmās' parasols amidst mandārava flowers.
In the midst of joyful and delighted gods, he stood amidst the whisks of his ascetic virtues (dhuta),
rejoicing manifoldly through divine forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and touches.
Amidst divine and delightful dances and instrumental music,
his qualities being praised by many thousands of verses,
he reached his sixteenth year and stood in the midst of the assembly of his kinsmen.
Having displayed every craft that exists in the world at that time,
gladdening the assembly of kinsmen as well as gods and humans,
he obtained Queen Yasodharā, who was of a noble lineage and perfectly suited to him.
Adorned with a gentle countenance resembling a golden mirror,
with large and long eyes like blue lotuses,
and a pair of eyebrows like banners at the gateway of the temple of beauty.
Her nose was like a golden trumpet in its beautiful form;
her dark, wavy hair was tied with a jeweled fillet at both ends like a mass of clouds;
and her lovely ears were adorned with earrings that shone like perpetual circles of lightning.
Her pair of jar-like breasts possess a luster like that of refined gold;
her necklace has the appearance of a waterfall descending from a golden mountain slope;
and her two arms resemble young shoots clinging to the celestial tree of her body.
With fingers like sprouting leaves, water-like palms, and rows of nails beautiful with dots;
adorned with a line of body-hair resembling a swarm of bees;
and variegated by three folds like waves upon the ocean of her form.
Her beautiful pair of thighs was encircled like golden plantain stems;
her lovely shanks were adorned with the graceful form of a closed kalikā bud;
she was the personification of visible beauty, resembling a mass of playful grace.
A virtuous mine of excellences, like the ocean at the time of its tide;
beloved like the king of spring, handsome like Kandappa;
beautiful to behold like the moon, and radiant with splendor like the sun.
Immovable like Mount Meru, deep as the ocean,
with a voice like that of Brahmā, speaking kindly and peerless in wisdom—
while that Great Hero was dwelling in the city of Kapilavatthu,
Having seen the four signs on the way to the park,
the Lord, delighting in the going-forth, went to the grounds of the park,
which was adorned with blossoming campaka, asoka, and nāga trees.
Abounding with full-blown lotuses and white water-lilies, agitated by the play of the waves,
scented by various fragrances brought by the gentle, slow-moving breeze,
and frequented by bees that have gathered from lake to lake.
Resounding with the songs of flocks of birds pure with fruit and flowers,
constantly echoing with the dances of intoxicated peacocks,
it was like a pleasure pavilion where herds of deer frolic and play.
Having come to the garden grove, which was excellent and brought joy to the people with rows of fountain-pavilions whose waters were vast and cool with sprays from the wind—
just as the King of the Devas [Indra] goes to the Nandana grove.
While playing, having heard the news that his son was born,
he turned back— adorned like the thousand-eyed Sakka accompanied by Vissakamma—
and as if entering a city, he heard the words spoken by Kisā Gotamī.
Having heard those words, which were pleasing to the heart and expressed a state of Nibbāna, he— contented and full of affection—
sent her a necklace worth a hundred thousand, radiant with bright gems, and then returned to his own palace.
He sat upon the excellent throne with the splendor of a king of the gods;
then many female dancers approached and surrounded him,
while some women among them took up and struck kettledrums.
Some sing songs filled with various melodies;
some blow into wind instruments, and others play stringed lutes.
With beautiful lips like bimba fruits and lovely, heavy breasts, they are radiant.
Then, broad-eyed with dark pupils and possessing faces as gentle as the moon,
they danced before him in the midst of the circle of drums,
like celestial maidens on a stage, absorbed incessantly in the aesthetic sentiment of the heroic.
Having seen that marvel, he then became dispassionate toward sense objects;
he beheld the beating of the heart and the beating of the drum at the end of all things;
and he perceived lamentation and song within the ocean of saṃsāra.
Like one dancing with a feverish agitation, the Leader thought:
"When shall I abandon my home and don the glory of the going-forth?
Thinking thus, he lay there as if asleep.
"He, depending upon whom we were occupied here with dancing and singing, he now sleeps soundly; whom shall we serve now?
Thinking thus, they [desisted] there from their respective musical instruments.
The young women lay there, unconscious and dependent on one another for awareness;
some were gnawing at their own teeth, others were drooling saliva,
some were weeping there, and still others were wailing.
Some cackle and swallow phlegm, while others vomit and cry out;
they make a noise at the nose and spit, saying "gharu";
then some urinate and wander about in secret.
That place smelled foul, like a raw corpse in a cemetery;
having awakened at midnight and gone there,
he sat down and then beheld their many transformations.
As he was thus contemplating, his mind became filled with spiritual urgency, and the three realms of existence appeared to him as if set ablaze—
just like an elephant in a vast forest that has been caught by a spreading wildfire.
In that same way, the king’s mind was set on departing from his palace;
then, rising from his bed and making his exit,
the great king reflected upon seeing his own son.
Having entered that chamber slowly and with a tranquil mind,
he beheld Yasodharā sleeping with her son,
while she herself maintained in her heart a great love for him who had returned after so long an absence.
Thinking, "Even after becoming a Buddha, it will be possible to see him," the Protector departed from that place with his mind fixed on enlightenment. Who, longing for Buddhahood,
would not have thought at that very moment, "I shall become a Buddha"?
As if lifting up Mount Sineru, he stepped out after having the hoof-ornaments removed;
calling for Channa, he had the horse Kanthaka, the lord of steeds, brought to him,
and mounting that king of horses together with Channa in the night, he departed.
The gods opened the gates, and he set out upon the great path.
Deities from many world-systems gathered together and honored him with lamps,
incense, banners, flags, perfumes, and garlands.
In front, sixty thousand held up torches on staffs;
likewise on the right side, the left side, and behind;
six deities caused showers of flowers to rain down from the sky.
The mandārava, the kokanada, the fragrant cittapāṭali;
the campaka, the asoka, the punnāga, and those produced from the nāga and pūga trees;
and those produced from various creepers such as the mālatī and vassikī.
A rain of flowers— lotuses, water-lilies, white lilies,
and others born from the water— fell over the beautiful land for thirty yojanas,
resounding with the humming of swarms of bees intoxicated by the fragrant nectar.
There the horse, overcome with distress,
then proceeded; thus, by means of these offerings, he went to the great river Anomā,
which was strewn with cool sprays and teeming with many kinds of fish.
Standing on the bank, that wise man saw the river Gaṅgā carrying its waters,
shining with its waves and offering a tribute of blue-lotus flowers;
having caused the great horse Mahānoma to leap across it, the one of great intelligence—
He established himself on the opposite shore upon a spotless expanse of sand;
thinking, "It is fitting for me to go forth right here,
I must not delay," he shed his radiance and cast off his ornaments.
Having prepared [the meal] for Channa and [provided] Kanthaka, the lord of horses, the Protector took up his sharp sword and cut off his matted locks; thus reflecting:
"If I am to be a Sugata," he thought.
"Let it remain suspended in the sky," he said, and threw up his garment.
Then Sakka, having received it in a costly jeweled casket and brought it to his head, proceeded toward the city of the gods.
Having had a jeweled stupa constructed and having enshrined that hair-relic therein,
the one of great intelligence honored it in many ways together with the Sahadevas for eight days, using the requisites brought by Mahābrahmā.
Having accepted it, the Leader then put on the saffron robe;
as before, having taken his own garment, he cast it into the sky.
Brahmā, having received it, went to the city of Brahmā.
Having constructed a beautiful, excellent stupa twelve yojanas in height,
he always placed it there with prostrations;
his mental aspirations fulfilled, he attained the glory of the going-forth.
Shrouding the earth as if with a veil of mist, the Leader strode forth;
then, having gone to the mango grove and finding the bliss of rapture,
he spent seven days in a delightful bower of trees.
Then, having gone to Rājagaha and donned his robe,
he— holding his jewel-colored bowl in his lotus-like palm,
endowed with the thirty-two marks and adorned with the secondary characteristics— [proceeded].
With body erect, the Blessed One approached the best of cities;
seeing the Sole Eye of the World passing through the middle of the street, the people thought thus: "This is not that lord of men."
"O moon-like young woman of the city,
it is our opinion that this moon has come today because of its connection to the lunar cycle,
not out of love for us. Having heard those words, some then laughed and spoke further:
"This is not the moon with its hare-mark; it is the sun, such is our thought"—
yet he has come, at will, to awaken the lotus-faces of the city women,
causing wonder among the citizens by his very form as a human being.
"O sirs, what madness is this? Do not speak thus now!
This is not the sun with its hundred rays and its hot beams; it is the one who has come to the city to sport with beings languid with desire."
"We have no doubt in our minds regarding his appearance.
Having heard those words of theirs, some people laughed and said, "Indeed, you do not know him;
he is one who possesses both arrows and a bow."
"The Lord, in a beautiful form, has arrived at this city atop the lofty palace known as Kelāsa; abandon your doubt in this matter.
Having heard their words, some people then laughed.
This is not Hara with three eyes;
he who has hair for his garment has come here seeking Fortune today, having approached the best of cities.
We believe he is in another guise; of this we have no doubt.
Having struck his hand and heard those words, some men laughed and said:
"This is certainly not Vāsudeva;
though he has the lotus-navel, he is a dwarf with a dark complexion."
The one of great splendor has arrived, bringing the manifest teaching, having come by means of a certain color;
thinking this city to be like the city of the gods,
he has promised to let it be seen— let your honors not lament!
Having heard their words, some made various jests:
"You do not know Sakka, for he, sirs, has the thunderbolt as his weapon;
this, sirs, is Mahābrahmā, who has come here from the Brahma-world."
"O Brahmins, why do you, who were once respected here, now speak thus out of negligence?
Having heard these words, those of a wise nature said:
'These are not Canda and the others; O sirs, do not proclaim such lust and delusion!'"
This Great Brahmā is four-faced, with a countenance as gentle as the moon;
this Brahmā Samantapothika is wonderful, with a bowl in his hand.
Indeed, O you whose merit is perfected through the perfections, this man is highly praised.
"Always revere, worship, and praise him of great splendor!"—
saying this, all those citizens followed after that Supreme Person,
honoring him with perfumes and flowers and paying him homage.
While the Munis were gliding upon the ocean of forms by means of their nets and oars,
living beings— those who use the boat of conceit— did not then see the further shore.
At that time, the Sole Eye of the World, walking in regular succession through the streets, [proceeded].
Having obtained just enough for his sustenance, the Sage, that bull among men, went outside the city and approached Mount Paṇḍava; there,
spreading out his outer robe in the shade of that mountain, he sat down.
Having seen mixed food in his bowl—something never seen before—he felt revulsion;
having spat it out, he reflected upon it.
Then, as if eating ambrosia, he rinsed his mouth with water.
Having performed his duties at the alms-bowl, he rested there for a moment;
King Bimbisāra, the lord of men, having observed that occurrence,
quickly approached him, and being granted permission, sat down.
Having invited him to sovereignty, when the Lord of Ascetics remained unwilling,
it was fitting for him to come to me as a Buddha out of favor toward me;
thus invited by him, the Greatly Wise One consented.
He of incomparable and vast prowess arrived at Uruvelā;
having exerted himself in the most difficult striving for six years,
he proclaimed to the world that there is no liberation [attained] by that means.
From that time forth, maintaining himself with a middling degree of effort,
the Great Sage, having provided sustenance for his body, then withdrew his faculties at the foot of the Ajapāla-nigrodha tree.
He sat there, illuminating every direction with his own splendor.
At that time, in the town of Senāni, Sujātā, the giver of milk,
her heart's desire fulfilled, made a request to the deity of the banyan tree.
"O Wise One," they thought, "the god is pleased, joyful, and delighted.
Having given a golden bowl filled with rice porridge, they spoke these words:
"O Great God, just as my aspiration has been fulfilled through your power,"
"May your intention likewise be fulfilled quickly.
Having spoken thus, and having paid homage and circumambulated her, Sujātā departed;
the Wise One, for his part, took up the bowl.
Having approached the exceedingly beautiful river Nīlavāhinī and sat down at the river landing named Suppatiṭṭhita,
he consumed his meal, having made it into fewer than fifty mouthfuls.
Having cast the bowl back upstream, the Bull among Men then rested day after day in the Sālavana grove; there,
having seen five dreams, he reflected upon their meaning.
On the path leading to the foot of the Bodhi tree, adorned by the gods with jeweled archways,
rows of pillars, full water-jars, banners, and other ornaments,
the Protector proceeded toward the Bodhi tree at the hour of evening.
Having seen the supreme bird named Sotthiya being honored,
he took eight handfuls of dark-green grass given by him,
approached the foot of the Bodhi tree, and circumambulated it.
Then he prepared a triple-layered seat facing the east;
thereafter, having split the earth in two, he rose upon the great throne—
high by fourteen cubits and variegated with diverse patterns.
"Let not my head split open, nor let me fall right there— thus firm of mind,
let skin, sinews, and bones remain;
let my limbs wither away, and let all my flesh and blood dry up."
"Having awakened, I shall not rise; I shall not abandon my effort.
Having thus resolved, he sat upon the diamond throne, establishing his conduct so that it could not be transgressed by any other conduct.
Placing his wrist against hers like a lotus against a lotus,
and resting her hand upon the palm of his own hand, the Jina placed her downcast eyes upon the young *asoka* leaf to which she was attached, or rather, upon another *asoka* sprout.
Just as a lofty mountain of gold kissed by the rays of twilight,
its slopes resplendent draped in robes of deep red,
shines like the sun itself blazing at the peak of the eastern horizon.
Adorned with a radiant facial orb shining above his shoulders,
like a deep blue lion’s cage upon a cloud of refined gold,
he had beautiful eyes half-closed, shielded by unblinking lashes.
He touched the trunk of the Bodhi tree, which was bound with a stalk of reed and adorned with a cluster of blue lotuses that eclipsed the beauty of women’s eyes;
and seated there, he cut away [the branches] from the Bodhi tree, which possessed young sprouts like coral.
Like a mass of fire falling upon those of evil intellect,
the gods of the ten thousandfold world-system quickly gathered there—
along with those seated on lotuses, the uragas, and the siddhas, vidyādharas, and others.
Sahampati Mahābrahmā, preceded by his host of Brahmās and holding a white sunshade,
stood near the Fully Enlightened One;
it was twenty hundred ratanas in height and named Vijayuttara.
Suyāma, the one who proclaims the ripening [of karma], stood respectfully blowing his conch shell together with his army,
praising the lord of men while holding a jeweled palm-leaf fan and fanning him very gently.
Jitakitti stood there, delighted, having grasped a peacock-feather fan at the tip of a flowering *latā* creeper;
he took up a *beluva* lute and sang a song following various musical modes.
Pañcasikha stood there, singing in many ways;
and Mahākāla, the lord of nāgas, surrounded by a host of nāgas,
stood there praising him with his ninefold virtues and other qualities.
Having measured out the arena and taken hold of a beautiful woman,
Timbaru, whose splendor was like the sun, stood there making his offering;
then Sitaṅga, adorned with white ornaments, arrived together with his army.
Dhataraṭṭha stood in the east, providing protection;
Virūḷhaka, filling the south with his own army, provided protection;
Nīlaṅga, adorned with blue ornaments, stood there providing protection.
Virūpakkha also stood guarding the western quarter,
adorned with red-hued ornaments and armor, preceded by his own army;
while in the northern quarter, he provided protection together with his host.
Naravāhana stood there, adorned with golden-colored ornaments.
What need is there for much talk here? The deities did not come to the field of his birth;
rather, they all arrived right here and brought him along.
When the one whose banner surpasses the sky touched the surface of the earth with his feet, even the nagas and other beings were not shaken;
what need then to speak of the banner itself?
Nor was it shaken by the feet of the standard, which move with the unrestrained force of the wind.
We speak of stars in the sky; but what indeed is the "bannered-ness" therein?
The eastern direction consists of the Cakkavāḷa mountains with their uplifted peaks, and the bases and other parts of those Cakkavāḷa mountains.
The world-systems, Mount Meru, Yugandhara, and other mountains were there,
fashioned in various colors like clusters of flowers;
beautiful with a profusion of drops of nectar from the left and right [petals].
The sky was your canopy, strewn with tossing lotuses;
there, by the gods, Brahmās, and others, scattered powders of sweet fragrance,
which appeared like a canopy within the pavilion at the summit of the world-system.
“May it not be that we think, ‘What can we say? while covered by black incense-piles rising here and there from the camphor and aloe-wood incense;
nor [may we think so] because of the abundant flowers and other offerings made by the devas in the birth-fields.”
Oh, how the earth is relieved of its burden! How great is the power of the quarters of the sky!
The flower garlands suspended from the heavens illuminate the surface of the earth like ropes stretched by the gods for the purpose of pulling it upward.
Seizing one another by the hand, the daughters of the gods wander through the sky,
singing delightful songs here and there;
with both arms outstretched, the daughters of the gods are adorned.
In every direction, pairs of celestial chariots shone like shimmering ornaments in the sky;
and divine maidens, holding clusters of blue lotuses and other flowers,
stood surrounding and worshipping the Lord of Men.
In the sky, celestial beauties, having taken golden and other jars filled with fragrant water—
abounding in lotuses and blue lilies, entwined with jeweled sprouts and pearl necklaces,
strewn with blossoms, and overflowing with water— [moved through] the atmosphere.
Having placed the Sugata in their midst, they worshipped him from all sides;
some stood there with golden fly-whisks in their hands,
while other goddesses stood holding palm-leaf fans.
Some stood surrounding the Jina, uttering words of auspicious connection with your aspiration,
crying out the praise of its fulfillment; they held aloft the eight supreme auspicious symbols, beginning with the śrīvatsa.
Standing in the sky, surrounding the voice of the Sage,
some women danced, some played, some sang, and some sported;
some played musical instruments, some sang, and some performed rhythmic clapping.
Rows of flower-offerings and likewise rows of lamp-offerings,
as well as rows of offerings adorned with jewels and gold,
ascending as far as the realm of Brahmā all around the world-system.
During the Buddha’s festival of auspiciousness, rows of various archways stand glowing;
they are fashioned from the seven precious gems,
and some may be made of gold, ivory, or cloth.
The interior of the world-system was filled without interval by many parasols of various colors,
like a lake crowded with lotuses;
and here and there on the earth, rows of many radiant mechanical lamps shone.
The courtyard of the sky was filled with a net of stars;
above the Cakkavāḷa mountains, there were parasols interspersed with banners,
and right there, the gateways and jar-lamps stood without any gaps.
The world-system was filled with the sounds of various musical instruments, various songs, and many cries of "Well done!"— O,
how great is the majesty of that Buddha who performed such auspicious rites!
For who indeed can describe that preeminent worship with but a single mouth?
Even the Four-Faced One, the Thousand-Eyed One, the Serpent with two thousand eyes,
and even the Ten-Necked One— none of them are able to recount it all.
Thus, on that day, when the world was crowded with countless great festivals performed by gods, asuras, brahmas,
garuḍas, nāgas, and others, Māra beheld this earth.
Having addressed his noble son, he spoke thus with curiosity:
"O sir, all the celestial mansions appear empty and abandoned;
having left behind the city and its ramparts, where have they gone along with the gods?"
Why do you not know, O Māra? Today I am merely asleep.
This is Siddhattha, the son of Māyā and King Śuddhodana;
having fulfilled all the perfections (pāramīs), he has gone forth from home.
"Today you are seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree, thinking, 'I shall become a Buddha';
for the purpose of honoring you, ten thousand deities have gathered,
joyful and delighted, performing a great festival today."
"Is your hearing deaf? Has your vision failed you?
Do you not see the tops of the victory banners?
Do you not hear the tumult? Having heard those words of theirs, the Wicked One, the Ender, indeed [spoke].
Distressed and dejected, grieving for them, he said this:
"Alas! What a great decline for the cycle of existence!
Truly, the cycle of existence is without essence now that Siddhattha has passed away."
"Alas! The threefold world, once complete, has perished"—like a forest consumed by fire, O sir, it is now devoid of fortune;
the three worlds are without light, O sir, like a sunless day for an Asura.
The kingdom, this Veda, and the three worlds are my very essence;
yet this child Siddhattha, abandoning my domain, departs.
By the path he has taken, the multitudes of people are departing as well.
"He does not honor you, O son of Suddhodana.
Come, let us go; let us make Siddhattha 'Asiddhattha' (one whose purpose is unfulfilled).
Create for him a terrifying form—ugly, hideous, harsh, and difficult to behold."
"Scatter him with words alone, like chaff blown by the wind!
Hearing those words of his, Māra’s army assembled,
assuming various guises and equipped with diverse weapons.
Then Māra, one hundred and fifty yojanas in height,
having mounted Girimekhala, came swiftly with his army;
seeing him from afar with his host, the gods—
Terrified, they fled swiftly in every direction;
Brahmā quickly ran away with his parasol,
shrinking back, while Sakka, filled with alarm, ran off placing the conch shell upon his back.
Then Mahākāla, the lord of nāgas, submerged himself in the earth;
O timid one, Vattadattakara fell upon his own couch.
Abandoning the performance of worship, including the gods, they cried out, "Saṃ! Saṃ!"
When she had passed away, this world-system was then empty;
that region became devoid of splendor, unsightly, and discordant, strewn with many fallen articles of worship.
There the Sugata sat alone upon the adamantine throne,
blazing with his own glory like the sun over Yugandhara; unshakable,
fearless, and free from any bristling of the hair on his body.
Fearless as the lion-king before the deer and wild beasts on their path,

the quarters became shrouded in darkness, and a comet appeared in the heavens.

even the torches were visible, and a conflagration seemed to seize the quarters of the sky.
In the cloudless firmament, there suddenly appeared the streaks of Indra’s bow.
Flocks of crows, owls, and kites, as well as terrifying headless trunks,

"For it is not right that an elephant should go against an elephant, nor should he go against a mere wooden statue.
It is no great matter to scare him away; this is the time for it.
Thinking thus, he quickly built [the statue], filled with fury, equal in speed to the wind of the world's destruction.
Quickly uprooting the great trees in the sky and hurling them forth,

thus there was victory for that glorious, Perfectly Awakened One.
In the first battle with Māra, there was defeat for Māra;
considering the Charioteer of Men to be thus possessed of great majesty,

Thus was the first victory.

"Now, let me carry this ascetic away on a great flood;

All directions were sealed and enveloped in darkness;

Deep, broad, and fierce, the great flood approached the presence of the Conqueror;

others run about with necklaces fastened around their throats;

Some, seizing glowing iron balls, hurl them in many ways;
others, with eyes terrifying and lips bitten,

Licking their own tongues with clubs made of flesh,
other soldiers ran about in the guise of intoxicated serpents;
some drank blood, while others devoured raw flesh.

other Yakkhas, bearing terrifying masks and frowning faces, leaped, swayed, and ran about with blazing weapons.

spears, and lances, and with masses of javelins, swords, and discuses;

[a world] filled with flames issuing from many thousands of tusks,

with hundreds of thousands of iron clubs and other weapons in his hands,

Unshakable, that Sage thus exerted his own strength,

What is the use of the retinue of glory, what of power, and what of prosperity?
Why do they harbor such thoughts of "I am superior" and "I am equal"? What is the purpose of these things for them?
The path of the sun, the enemy of darkness, becomes elevated;
then the lotus-snakes, roaring and causing the elephants to trumpet,

Just as lions, when they come within the range of vision,

Thus those two armies, clashing with one another,
brandishing various weapons and shouting aloud,
were constantly agitated like the waves of the ocean tossing about.

at the end of that night’s watch, the Lord of Sages,

during the dark fortnight of the month of Madhu, on the day of the Uposatha.

With hands placed upon their heads like blooming red lotuses,

Then the Sage, in order to reconcile that conflict between the serpents—
Uttering a lovely, sublime voice, the one of excellent mind taught that supreme Dhamma to the serpents—
the well-praised path to the ageless and deathless,

O friends, in this saṃsāra there is indeed not even a grain of essence;
when will that distinction be found amidst the burning fire?
It constantly afflicts people with passion, disease, and manifold misfortunes.
Likewise, life is like the morning sun that shines directly toward one;
this body is a mass of thirty-two kinds of filth, devoid of essence;

Having abandoned this accumulated cycle of existence and non-existence that must be traversed—
who indeed would choose existence, O sir, when such is the case? For what wise man would be envious,

People from the past, O sir, fall into even more dreadful hells;
as snakes, jackals, hyenas, and monkeys, they are slain by one another many times over—
this is the suffering of conditioned existence, devoid of any benefit.
The pure crow, the owl, and then the *phandana* snake,
having committed evil in this place, have long experienced suffering and misfortune;

"There is not even an atom’s worth of satisfaction in quarreling, O sir; this so-called 'friendship' is nothing but death.

An elephant that is young and intoxicated is not a source of strength or refuge when it has entered [the fray];
why, O sirs, do you exert your vigor in an improper place?
For those who have abandoned quarreling and are of one mind, there is no suffering.
In the past, O Lāpas, you were unassailable and spoke kindly;
you lived happily as long as you remained free from harm.

Thus, with sharp wisdom, he exhorted them all together in the sublime Dhamma,

then those Nāgas, their minds gladdened, were filled with joy.

then the Sage, having ascended the vault of the sky like the young sun,

among those born of water and land who had come there for battle—
Countless tens of millions of serpents,
firmly established in the pure virtue of seeking refuge and being well-pleased,
performed a most sublime act of worship for the Teacher.

This region of the earth, strewn with blood,
appears to me like a blazing fire quenched by a rain-cloud;

O Ten-Powered One, we have previously seen your beautiful body,
overspread with a network of rays, as you taught the most sweet Dhamma to the gods,

Formerly, I was known to you as a slave;
if there is compassion in your heart for a slave once again,

"Because you possess these very elements of beauty like a radiant gem, therefore revere the Great One constantly, as I do; he grants both heaven and liberation.

Having ascended to the realm of the atmosphere,
the rays of blue, yellow, and other colors spread in every direction,

In the sixth year, the Sage made his dwelling in the most delightful forest grove named Maṅkula, the king of mountains; and then,

In his seventh year there, the Lord of Sages, Aruṇa,
shining upon the soft stone while teaching the most subtle Abhidhamma to the devas,

Then, in the eighth autumn, the Lord of Sages, the giver of happiness, possessed of stainless wisdom, dwelt in the monastery named Jetavana,
experiencing for others the peace that is ageless and deathless.
Teaching the Dharma, variegated by manifold methods—
such was the second visit to Laṅkā.
Thus the Conqueror, dwelling in Jetavana, remained there.
Relying upon the city of Sāvatthī, he dwelt there;
what was that city like at that time,
and what was that Jetavana monastery like?
Placed upon the head of the lady of the earth,
shining with the splendor of various jewels,
his broad coils appeared like a vast crown.
She was the delightful one in Jambudvīpa;
bringing glory to the abode of Śrī,
she shone resplendent upon the surface of the earth.
It was as delightful as Amarāvatī, the city of the king of the gods, or as Alakā, the city of King Kuvera;
it was inhabited by people who were devoted to merit and wisdom.
With streets strewn with gold coins and the like,
and resplendent with the majestic display of elephants and horses,
that row of golden mansions shines forth.
That radiant princess shone,
displaying the grace of her virtuous limbs, while the brahmins who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences attended upon her.
Constantly resounding with the sounds of the five kinds of musical instruments,
filled with hundreds of people skilled in many crafts,
it was thronged by caravan leaders who had arrived from various directions.
Purified by the feet of those who had attained the destruction of the taints,
she shone like a temple of auspiciousness— she who,
while wandering through other existences, practiced the holy life.
Relying on the Suva mountain, he dwelt there by virtue of his qualities;
he made the *yaññaṅga* tree— whose leaves were as dark as lead—
flourish with fruits and sprouts.
Now, having reached the end of existence,
who indeed could fully describe the virtues of that Lord of Sages who dwells there in dependence?
She spoke to her with the parable of the rain;
he was like an invaluable jewel brought near,
captivating and devoted to the highest beings.
The monastery known as Jetavana became a place where the swarms of bees were delighted by the nectar of flowers in full bloom.
Where trees stand like clever actors,
resonating with the humming of bees and the sound of lutes,
and filled with the songs of the warbling of infinite birds.
Having drawn milk from the ocean, washed it to remove the water,

That garland of flower-pavilions shone like a mass of clouds,

In which the rays emerging from the body of the Perfectly Enlightened One spread forth like lattices issuing from a forest of glowing coals,

Where the alms-gatherers dependent on ascetics shine,

asuras, devas, humans, nāgas, ascetics, and siddhas [dwell].
Where the hosts of Vidyādharas and others, having offered their salutations,
rejoice with the mere thought that they have arrived,
as they sing songs of auspicious praise proclaimed by those very beings.
With stainless, cool, and resonant waterfalls,
with reservoirs whose waters were proclaimed as pure by many birds,
and with stone surfaces strewn with flower filaments and fallen leaves.
Wherein ascetics always find delight; he who,
having abandoned the immeasurable and great glory of Kapilavatthu, [has left behind] a mass of merit accumulated over many hundreds of eons.
Wherever the Sugata, the Great Seer,
has taken refuge and found delight, what incomparable blessing does the Teacher proclaim there?
In that Jeta’s Grove monastery dwells the Victor.
Just as Rucira was in the Nandana grove,
or as Brahmā with the Grandfathers in the Brahma-abode,
so Vanda was surrounded by Tārāvalī in the sky.
Then the Great Naga, named Maṇiakkhika,
having approached from Laṅkā to the feet of the Victor, spread his hood and spoke thus:
"The Fully Enlightened Ones, O Wise One, appear in the world for the welfare and prosperity of the world."
"O Lord, we have been born as your boundless devotees;
therefore, for me who has become your servant, this firm prison of the miserable cycle of existence—
liberation from which you desire for me— is my invitation to be accepted."
Having heard that invitation from the Great Naga, he, the Great Naga,
accepted it by means of his silence out of compassion;
knowing this, the joyful Naga quickly returned to Siṃhala.
On the delightful ground beside the Kalyāṇa River,
in a place composed of silver, conch, pearl, coral, and diamond,
he had the foundation-pot and other items deposited for the great stupa worthy of being built.
Having given the scales and so forth, and likewise the remaining parts of the temple structure,
as well as the rows of *viṭaṅkas*, *vyālas*, lions, and the like— all beautifully fashioned with many variegated designs made of *sātakumha*— he gave them.
Having fashioned the rafters, the side-beams,
and the central ridge-pole; having constructed the pinnacle with a *nikkha* coin,
the finial with precious gems, and the golden tinkling garlands and ear-garlands;
Having stretched out a canopy and hung loose tassels here and there,
making it crowded with garlands of perfumes and garlands of flowers;
in the center was a priceless great throne made of sapphire.
He had beautiful seats constructed all around for the remaining monks;
he built a railing made of ivory for the resting place as if with jewels,
and a delightful courtyard strewn with sand of pearls.
Above the archway, which was fashioned from the seven precious gems,
were further arches strewn with santīra flowers and crowded with golden jars and the like;
it was beautifully adorned with canopies covered in many-colored banners.
Having constructed a most excellent pavilion, peaceful as the pavilions of the gods,
adorned with many such descriptions—
strewn with lamps and incense, and filled with fragrant flowers;
Having thus fashioned a great highway, smooth and perfectly even, covered with cool sand and soft as a foot-cloth,
those elephants gathered together various kinds of edible and chewable fruits.
At that time, when divine food and drink were abundant, they were traveling along the path back. Then,
on the eighth week from his enlightenment,
on the full moon day of Vesākha, the Compassionate Lord gathered his disciples together.
"Today, O monks, let us go to Laṅkā for the benefit of the Nāgas;
Maṇiakkhika, having placed his faith in the Buddha’s teaching, has invited us.

took his bowl and robes and went into the presence of the Conqueror;
so too did the one named Mahākassapa, who had shaken off evil and was foremost in the ascetic practices.

he who was known as Āpalika, an expert in the Vinaya of the Teaching,

The path of those with the divine eye— Anuruddha, the elder, the bestower of boons,
who has restrained evil enemies and is free from pride— went into the presence of the Sage,
renowned as one who fulfills desires like a wish-fulfilling gem.
Then the wise Bakkula, a leader of the community, worthy of offerings, a disciple of the Elder Jinantika,

arrived with his requisites at the assembly of monks.
The Elder Aṅgulimāla, a bearer of the Buddha’s Dispensation,
equipped himself and went forth at once to come into the presence of the Lord of Munis;
he shines like the sun upon the peak of Mount Udaya, the rising of the Dispensation.
Thus this Elder Rāhula also went quickly to his father’s presence;
and the Elder named Bhaddiya, of auspicious conduct, like a vessel of blessings,
having become renowned throughout the world, also went into the presence of the Fully Awakened One.
Like the celestial tree that grants whatever is desired to the world, he who is called Selabhu,
a son of the Conqueror, went into the presence of the Fully Enlightened One;
like the lord of the night, he shines in the sky of the Dispensation.
The great elder Mahānāma approached the presence of the Sage;
like a lion yawning upon the surface of the Manosilā rock,
the great elder named Subhūti came into the presence of the Buddha.
Like a crane at the Chaddanta lake in the Buddha’s dispensation,
the renowned Elder Tissa also went to the assembly of monks;
he was like a bee dwelling in the midst of the blossoming lotuses of the Victor’s teaching.
The Elder Rādha, resembling a bee, also went forth at once;
so too did Bhagu, Dabba, Upasena, Koṇḍañña, Assaji, and Sīvali— these elders,

Kumārakassapa, Puṇṇa, Soṇa, Upasena, Revata—
these renowned elders went into the presence of the Teacher;
as did Vaṅgīsa, Sāgata, Nanda, Bhāradvāja, and Gavampati.
Taking their bowls and robes, they went into the presence of the Victor;
in this manner, five hundred great Nāgas,
the sons of the Victor, came together with the Sage to visit the Lord of the World.
Then he, the joy of the world, moved by compassion,
like Mount Meru encircled by many-colored lightning flashes,
dressed himself in a radiant robe that scattered rays of pure light.
Above that, the Victor fastened a red waist-band;
as if concealing the Great Stupa— which rose up loftily with the lovely luster of gold—
with a cloak of red woolen cloth;
Having made the saṅghāṭī robe from dust-heap rags as bright red as a ripe banyan fruit,
and having made it a well-fitted upper garment,
he put it on properly and wore it with great care.
The Conqueror, whose hand was like a lotus, extended it, adorned with a web of lines;
by the power of the Lord of the World, the honey fell from the bowl,
and as it reached the interior of his lotus-like hand, he took it.
Then the Protector, together with his disciples, rose into the expanse of the sky and proceeded,
crushing the clouds of various colors there;
then, from the body of the Sambuddha, six rays of light issued forth.
From his golden ears, like jeweled rafters,
the stars— blue as blue-lotus flowers and emeralds—
seemed to cover the Sage’s body as if with blossoms.
With garlands of campaka flowers and golden powder upon their garments,
they fill the wide-open space before the Victor’s body with yellow threads;
and with clusters of bhaṇḍī flowers and rubies, they adorn it.
Red light radiated from the Sage’s body, filling the quarters and intermediate directions;
with necklaces, jasmine garlands, and strings of crystal and other gems,
they were filled from the Sage’s body, pure white and unattached.
With masses of topaz and rubies, and with lotus-hued gems,
the radiance of the Victor’s body covered the quarters like a day filled with many rainbows and adorned by the rising sun.
From the limbs of the Conqueror, rays of six colors— like a variegated cloth being released from the body of the Victor—
rush forth like mountain peaks or gabled chambers,
shimmering as they strike one another at the boundary of their garlands.
While traveling, having struck against the mountain ridges of the world-system,

While the horses were prancing about, displaying their own beauty,
the clouds were then colored by the upward-rising rays; once more,
the solar disc appeared as if newly formed, in various hues.
The goddesses who had been submerged in the streams of the Jinappahā vanished;
at that time, they must have appeared in various colors as if to pay homage with their own splendors.
Then, the daughters of the gods entered into the midst of the Buddha’s rays.
The gods, asuras, nāgas, brahmās, siddhas, vidyādharas, and others were momentarily bewildered and lost consciousness regarding their own husbands;
yet they honored the Conqueror with yak-tail whisks, parasols, and banners.
Some arranged rows of costly [offerings] upon the arches and above the arches;
they placed lines of water-jars and lamps all around on every side;
they spread out foot-cloths and stretched out canopies.
There above, they scattered many flowers, wondering:

"Where indeed does the God of Gods go?

Having fashioned jeweled pavilions on the paths on all sides, they wait.
Having prepared the lodgings, some deities remain there,

those who behold the Conqueror there together with his disciples, shimmering with glory—

may there be satisfaction for all Tathāgatas at all times!

Then the Ganges, having approached that charming pair along with their son,
took them by the lotus-feet with her tender wave-arms.

He arrived at the beautiful pavilion that brought delight to the mind;
having gone to the center of the pavilion, he sat upon the great throne worthy of a Buddha,

they made the pavilion appear exceedingly radiant, like a lake crowded with lotuses. Having approached, those whose eyes were like lotuses took their places before the Teacher, whose face was as lovely as a lotus.

Thus has the Jina taught this Dhamma for those such as Anilāsana and others—teaching that generates rapture and joy and brings the nectar of Nibbāna:
"O, O serpents, listen! In the ocean of existence..."
In this difficult passage, crowded with crocodiles, sharks, and sea-monsters,
when indeed will people find a firm footing on the path?
Having abandoned the vast ship of the Buddha, which possesses the solid essence of steadfastness;
Having obtained the appearance of the Sage, which is even more difficult to find,
the serpents did not indulge in negligence for a long time,
[fearing] birth, old age, death, suffering, and lamentation.
For those caught in saṃsāra who have not yet departed from it,
youth is but a brief moment— like the fleeting beauty of a lotus, or like a grain of frost,
more insubstantial than anything else for living beings.
The ocean displays the play of waves in its enjoyment,
yet the mind is constantly scorched by the various flames of sorrow;
even those of poor wisdom, having made the objects of passion their prey, become like birds [caught in a snare].
Even toward the *thirūpi* flower,
those greedy for form have fallen away from their former meditative absorptions (*jhāna*).
Therefore, O you of excellent wisdom, do not be attached to form.
In former times, the peacock, though guarding his passion for sounds,
heard the sweet and melodious cry of the peahen and, with his body thrilled,
fell into the hands of the hunter; therefore, one should not be attached to the realms of existence.
There was indeed no sound that caused suffering to people;
leaving behind the passion for the pollen of many flowers, the elephant,
greedy for the scent of rut, proceeded toward the frontal globes of other elephants.
The bhiṅga flower is broken and thin, like the ear of an elephant;
there is nothing at all in the three worlds comparable to its fragrance,
even though it grows in deep waters and is covered by leaves.
The fool, having swallowed the hook out of greed for the bait,
experiences incomparable suffering; knowing that there is no true satisfaction in flavors, abandon greed for flavors, O people!
O, this pure being who has come from the Brahma-world,
destined indeed for Buddhahood— even though he were a Bodhisatta—
has fallen away from this goal because of his attachment to fame.
Therefore, indeed, there is no calamity equal to contact (phassa);
[even] Bheraṇḍa, Pelaka, Kapu’ddaka, and Hetuhīna— beings who delight in giving,
through the power of the jewel of their generosity— [are not affected by it].
Who that is wealthy would not bestow upon these serpents the city of Śiva—
the supreme essence of the realm of liberation—
after they have protected their stainless virtue, even though they are like venomous snakes?
She was the beloved chief queen in Indra’s Nandana Grove;
